S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
examples: Makes mistakes in homework or tests by misreading questions or skipping important parts.
Frequently omits details or makes typos in work documents or reports.
Repeats mistakes in calculations or numerical work, such as switching signs or getting digits wrong.
Performs tasks incorrectly by missing important details in instructions.

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
examples: Unable to engage in calm activities for long, such as reading quietly or drawing.
Cannot play quietly, often shouting or making loud noises during games or play.
Unable to stay quiet in quiet places like libraries or movie theaters, making noise.
Cannot endure and avoids quiet and calm activities like meditation or yoga.

S014.name: Constant_Activity
S014.description: Is often 'on the go', acting as if 'driven by a motor'.
examples: Constantly moving and active as if driven by a motor.
Starts another task immediately after finishing one, without resting for a moment.
Unable to stay still even on weekends or days off, constantly doing something.
Appears to others to be always busy and bustling about.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
examples: Cannot wait and cuts in line or gets impatient when standing in a queue.
Rushes or cuts in without waiting for their turn in games or board games.
Keeps checking the time or complaining when waiting for their turn at hospitals or public offices.
Fidgets, complains, or gets annoyed in situations where waiting for a turn is required.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
examples: Butts into conversations of others where they have not been invited.
Joins in on others' work or games without permission or interferes.
Touches or uses other people's belongings or work without permission.
Keeps talking to and disturbing others when they are focusing on work or studying.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattentive and hyperactive‑impulsive behaviors that are inconsistent with developmental level and cause clear functional impairment across settings (e.g., school, work, home). Symptoms typically begin in childhood, though they may not be fully recognized until academic or occupational demands increase, and they often persist into adolescence and adulthood with changing manifestations (e.g., internal restlessness rather than overt running/climbing). The clinical course is usually chronic, with fluctuating severity influenced by structure, motivation, and environmental supports. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and learning disorders by the early onset, cross‑situational nature of attention and impulse‑control difficulties, and by the presence of characteristic hyperactive‑impulsive features rather than solely situational or stress‑linked concentration problems.

patient.stressor: For most of his career, Baha’s energy and willingness to jump into action were seen as assets in the firehouse, and the highly structured, adrenaline‑driven nature of calls helped mask underlying attention and impulse‑control issues. About a year and a half ago he began taking on more leadership responsibilities and promotional coursework toward captaincy, which required detailed report writing, classroom learning, and careful adherence to evolving protocols outside the high‑intensity emergency setting. During this period he received repeated feedback about incomplete paperwork, missed details in incident narratives, and disruptive side conversations during training sessions, culminating in a formal warning after a near‑miss where he overlooked a critical checklist item during a drill. Concerned that these recurring lapses could endanger colleagues and stall his promotion, and after a trusted battalion chief suggested an evaluation rather than framing it as a character flaw, Baha sought psychiatric care to understand why staying focused and organized at this level of responsibility felt so unmanageable.
patient.chief_complaint: “When I’m not on an actual call, I just can’t keep my attention on training, reports, or manuals long enough to get through them properly.”

S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
S001.manifestation: With these incident reports, I’ll swear I’ve gone over them carefully, but then my lieutenant points out I wrote the wrong street number or skipped a whole section, like my eyes just slid right over it even though I thought I was being careful.

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: Unless we’re talking about an active fire, my brain taps out after maybe ten minutes in class or reading protocols—I catch myself staring at the same paragraph over and over with nothing actually sticking, and I feel almost physically unable to force my attention back on it.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: I’ll start a report or an online module with good intentions, get halfway through, click over to check an email or talk to someone, and then realize at the end of the shift—or the end of the week—that I never went back and finished it, even when I know people are waiting on me.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: When I’m trying to work on paperwork at the station, the smallest thing—a radio crackle, somebody joking in the bay, even my own random thought about what I’m cooking for dinner—pulls me completely off task, and ten minutes later I’m in a whole different conversation or googling something with the form still blank in front of me.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: Lately I’m constantly forgetting everyday stuff like calling my wife back, paying a bill I set on the counter, or even showing up to a rescheduled training, not because I don’t care, but because the second it’s out of sight it just falls right out of my head.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: Sitting in those longer training sessions, I’m bouncing my leg, tapping my pen, twisting my ring, shifting in the chair the whole time, and even when I try to hold still I last maybe a minute before something on me is moving again without me even noticing.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
S012.manifestation: Any time I’m stuck in a chair for more than a few minutes without action—like during classroom lectures or long briefings—I get this pent‑up, crawling feeling inside, like I have to stand up and pace or I’m going to jump out of my skin.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
S013.manifestation: Even on my days off, I can’t just sit quietly and read or watch a movie with my son without talking over it, fiddling with my phone, or getting up to do something else, because being quiet and still like that makes me feel edgy and bored within minutes.

S014.name: Constant_Activity
S014.description: Is often 'on the go', acting as if 'driven by a motor'.
S014.manifestation: My crew jokes that I’m powered by batteries because I’m always moving—if I’m not on a call I’m reorganizing gear, wiping something down, checking the trucks again, or pacing the hallways, and I don’t really know how to just sit and relax unless I’m completely exhausted.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
S017.manifestation: When there’s a line—at the store, waiting for medicals at the clinic, or even when guys are taking turns practicing a skill—I get really impatient, checking the time, biting back the urge to jump ahead or tell people to hurry up because it feels like torture to just stand there and wait.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
S018.manifestation: I keep catching myself cutting people off mid‑sentence in meetings or jumping into conversations at the firehouse that I wasn’t really part of, and I’ll answer questions the instructor hasn’t even finished asking because the thought pops into my head and I blurt it out before I can stop myself.

add_requirements.onset_prior_to_12_years: Even back in elementary school my teachers were always moving my seat because I wouldn’t stop talking, I’d forget to turn in homework I actually did, and every report card mentioned that I was smart but couldn’t sit still or stay focused in class.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: Since taking on more leadership and coursework, these issues have led to formal write-ups, a near-miss during a drill, and me falling behind on the promotional track because my officers don’t trust me to handle the detailed paperwork and protocols without extra oversight.
add_requirements.duration: These problems with staying focused, finishing tasks, and sitting still have really come to a head and been impossible to ignore ever since I started the captaincy coursework about a year and a half ago.
